text: Technology Layer 1 universe should remain decomposed across physical AI infrastructure, semiconductor subsupply, optical networking, power/grid, cyber control planes, and automation rather than collapsing into mega-cap AI leaders.
HBM and advanced-packaging subsupply currently has the strongest evidence base, especially inspection/metrology, wafer-level test, bonding, OSAT capacity, and process-control equipment.

Data-center electrical equipment and power infrastructure are high-priority Technology chokepoints because AI cluster deployment depends on switchgear, transformers, turbines, grid interconnection, and permitting.

Optical networking remains a priority discovery lane, but current Layer 1 evidence is weaker and needs primary-source validation for 800G/1.6T, InP, lasers, optical engines, and customer qualifications.

Cybersecurity and automation should remain in the Technology funnel as lower-confidence software/control-plane and factory-productivity lanes, but they need stronger evidence of unavoidable customer dependency.

Layer 2 must add primary-source company validation: filings, transcripts, investor presentations, backlog, book-to-bill, customer concentration, named customer evidence, analyst coverage, market cap, liquidity, and falsification triggers.

Current universe is U.S.-listed heavy; next searches should deliberately expand Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, Europe, and Israel for substrates, materials, inspection, bonding, photonics, power equipment, and automation suppliers.

For the Technology theme, use AI infrastructure as the initial mapped subtheme: demand begins with AI workloads and hyperscaler/neocloud capex, but hidden bottlenecks are more likely in advanced packaging, HBM test, inspection/metrology, substrates, power distribution, cooling, and process inputs.

Highest-priority bottleneck nodes for later layers: ABF film/substrates, HBM probe-card and known-good-die test, advanced-package inspection/metrology, high-end AI-server MLCCs, and data-center switchgear/electrical systems.

Low-attention nodes worth deliberate follow-up: semiconductor process chemicals, semicap subsystems, component distributors/allocation channels, customer qualification gates, thermal-management subcomponents, and power-delivery passives.
Supplier earnings that disclose AI, HBM, advanced-packaging, data-center, or high-end component revenue mix should be treated as the main validation catalyst for Layer 2B and Layer 3.
Large customer advance payments, co-funded capacity expansions, or long-term supply agreements are strong indicators that buyers see a node as hard to replace.

Need primary-source verification for all non-cached claims from Substack or commentary sources: company filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, customer announcements, and official order/backlog disclosures.

Need to separate true bottlenecks from cyclical rebound: check whether revenue growth, backlog, margins, or capacity utilization are specifically tied to AI infrastructure rather than broad semiconductor or industrial recovery.

Need to avoid high-attention mega-cap dominance: TSMC, hyperscalers, GPU vendors, and major memory vendors should remain reference anchors, while discovery should focus on smaller suppliers, tools, components, materials, distributors, and certification gates.

CAMT should remain in the underfollowed inspection/metrology lane for AI advanced packaging and HBM, with promotion dependent on primary-source evidence of sustained HBM or heterogeneous-integration order mix, repeat customers, backlog conversion, and margin resilience.

FORM should remain in the underfollowed HBM wafer-level probe-card / known-good-die test lane, with the key verification being whether HBM probe-card revenue is growing faster than legacy DRAM, NAND, foundry/logic, or systems revenue.
ONTO should remain in the underfollowed HBM bump metrology and advanced-packaging process-control lane, but its large-cap status means the evidence bar should be higher than for smaller candidates.

POWL should be tracked as a separate AI physical-infrastructure chokepoint rather than a semiconductor subsupply name; provided evidence on backlog, book-to-bill, and data-center order size makes it one of the strongest current hard-evidence relationships in this chunk.

KLIC belongs in the underfollowed bonding-equipment lane, but its thesis should stay at hypothesis level until thermocompression, advanced dispense, or memory-packaging orders are shown to be material and specifically tied to HBM or AI accelerator packaging.

BESI.AS belongs in the hybrid-bonding / advanced-packaging equipment lane as a U.S.-underrepresented European supplier; its thesis requires verification of AI, HBM, or chiplet customer adoption, backlog, and tool lead-time constraints.
UCTT should remain a speculative_shadow candidate until filings show clear advanced-packaging or AI-driven WFE platform exposure, customer concentration benefits, backlog growth, and margin leverage.

AMKR and TSM should be used as reference anchors, not alpha candidates, to trace which upstream inspection, metrology, bonding, test, substrate, and materials suppliers are pulled into the AI advanced-packaging capacity expansion.

Primary-source verification is still missing for most company-level relationships. Next layer should pull 10-K/20-F/6-K filings, earnings transcripts, investor decks, backlog disclosures, customer concentration, segment revenue, product adoption, and capex supplier evidence.

Standard falsification triggers for this chunk: backlog decline, book-to-bill below 1.0, HBM/advanced-packaging order commentary fading, margin compression during backlog conversion, customer dual-sourcing, capacity additions by competitors, delayed hyperscaler capex, or AI package architecture changes that reduce inspection/probe/bonding intensity.
LITE mapped to AI optical-networking component chain as an underfollowed inference; direct evidence needed on datacom mix, 800G/1.6T, AI customers, margins, and capacity.
COHR mapped to AI optical-networking photonics/materials chain as an underfollowed inference; direct evidence needed on AI datacenter revenue, InP/laser constraints, and margin mix.
FN mapped to optical manufacturing and precision assembly as an underfollowed hypothesis; validate datacom/AI module revenue, customer concentration, capacity utilization, and dual-sourcing risk.
AAOI remains speculative_shadow for data-center transceivers; must verify named customer wins, 800G/1.6T qualification, gross margins, and balance-sheet durability.
POET remains speculative_shadow for co-packaged optics and optical engines; require proof of commercial shipments, qualifications, manufacturing partnerships, and cash runway.
VRT is a reference leader for AI data-center power and cooling infrastructure; monitor backlog, liquid cooling, AI datacenter mix, and margin sustainability.
ETN is a reference leader for data-center electrical equipment and power management; use as a benchmark for switchgear, backlog, lead times, and pricing.
GEV is a reference leader for power-generation and grid bottlenecks tied to AI data-center power availability; validate turbine/grid backlog and data-center relevance.
NVT mapped as an underfollowed data-center electrical balance-of-plant hypothesis; verify data-center mix, product criticality, lead times, order growth, and pricing.
ATKR mapped as an underfollowed second-order data-center construction input hypothesis; verify data-center mix and whether raceway/conduit demand has pricing power or is commoditized.
Optical-networking candidates in this chunk lack primary-source evidence tying revenue or backlog directly to AI clusters, 800G/1.6T deployments, hyperscaler qualifications, or capacity bottlenecks.
Electrical-infrastructure candidates beyond Powell require company-level primary evidence for data-center order growth, backlog duration, lead times, pricing, and AI-specific end-market exposure.
Balance-of-plant names NVT and ATKR may be obscure second-order beneficiaries, but they need product criticality and margin evidence before promotion in the Serenity funnel.

AVGO should remain a reference anchor rather than an underfollowed candidate; use it to trace custom AI accelerator and AI networking pull-through into substrates, advanced packaging, optical networking, switch ecosystems, power delivery, and test suppliers.

MU should remain a reference HBM anchor; its main Layer 2B value is mapping HBM capex and supply constraints into probe cards, wafer-level test, known-good-die, inspection, metrology, bonding, substrates, and advanced packaging.

TER is the most directly relevant underfollowed candidate in this chunk for semiconductor AI infrastructure because test intensity can rise with AI accelerator, HBM, and advanced-package complexity, but primary-source proof is still required.

CGNX and NOVT belong in an automation-components lane rather than a semiconductor bottleneck lane until filings show meaningful semiconductor/electronics, robotics, warehouse automation, or AI-enabled inspection exposure.

SYM belongs in a warehouse-automation systems lane with high deployment and customer-concentration diligence requirements; do not treat it as an AI infrastructure chokepoint without backlog quality and software-economics proof.

TENB and S are underfollowed cyber-control-plane hypotheses, but they require stricter evidence because software control planes are less physically scarce than chips, substrates, test, power, cooling, and electrical equipment.

NET and ZS should be retained as reference benchmarks for the cloud/cyber lane, not as underfollowed bottleneck names, unless future evidence shows AI workload monetization, mission-critical security dependence, and resilient retention.

Primary-source verification is missing for all names in this chunk. Next layer should pull 10-K/10-Q filings, earnings transcripts, investor decks, backlog/RPO data, segment revenue, customer concentration, AI-specific product disclosures, and margin trends.

Market-pricing checks are missing: current market cap, valuation multiples, revenue growth, margin expectations, analyst coverage, short interest, liquidity, and relative performance versus direct bottleneck peers need to be refreshed before prioritization.

Falsification triggers should include falling backlog or RPO, book-to-bill below 1 where applicable, AI revenue claims not converting to segment growth, margin compression, customer dual-sourcing, delayed hyperscaler capex, weaker DRAM/HBM pricing, and platform-vendor displacement in cyber.
